nameStory: These elegant birds get their name from two distinctive features: their love of cedar berries and the waxy red tips on their wing feathers. The red wing tips look remarkably like drops of old-fashioned red sealing wax, the kind once used to seal letters and important documents.
description: Cedar Waxwings are sleek, medium-sized songbirds with a refined, almost formal appearance. They're primarily soft brown and gray with yellow accents, sporting a distinctive black mask across their eyes and a bright yellow band at the tip of their tail. These social birds are about the size of a robin but more streamlined, with silky-smooth plumage that gives them an almost polished look.

idTips.label: Black eye mask
idTips.description: A distinctive black band runs through the eyes like a bandit's mask, contrasting sharply with the pale brown head

idTips.label: Yellow tail band
idTips.description: The tail ends in a bright yellow stripe that looks like it was dipped in paint, easily visible in flight

idTips.label: Red waxy wing tips
idTips.description: Small red dots on the wing tips that look like drops of bright red candle wax - though these may be absent on younger birds

idTips.label: Silky plumage
idTips.description: Feathers appear unusually smooth and polished, with a soft brown body that gradually shifts to gray on the wings and back

idTips.label: Crest and posture
idTips.description: Small pointed crest on the back of the head and an upright, alert posture when perched

idTips.label: Flocking behavior
idTips.description: Almost always seen in groups, moving together in tight formations with high-pitched trilling calls

habitat: Cedar Waxwings prefer open woodlands, parks, orchards, and suburban areas with plenty of fruit-bearing trees and shrubs. Look for them in areas with cedars, crabapples, serviceberries, and other berry-producing plants. They're equally at home in city parks and rural farmland edges, as long as there's a good mix of trees and open space.

seasonality.spring: Waxwings arrive in variable numbers and timing, often appearing suddenly in flocks around fruit trees. They may be building nests in late spring, later than most other songbirds.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when they're most likely to be seen in smaller family groups. Young birds lack the waxy red wing tips and may have streaky underparts.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks gather to feast on berries and fruits, making this an excellent time for observation. They're particularly drawn to crabapples, mountain ash, and late-ripening fruits.
seasonality.winter: Numbers vary greatly from year to year, but flocks may linger around reliable food sources like ornamental fruit trees and berry bushes that persist through cold weather.

funFact: Cedar Waxwings can actually get drunk from eating fermented berries, leading to erratic flying and sometimes fatal crashes into windows - they're one of the few birds known to experience intoxication just like humans do with alcohol!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with female cardinals from a distance, but cardinals have thick orange beaks and lack the yellow tail band and black mask. Remember: "Waxwings wear masks, cardinals have caps."
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, Cedar Waxwings don't exclusively eat cedar berries - they actually prefer a wide variety of fruits and berries. The "cedar" in their name comes from their fondness for the small blue berries of Eastern Red Cedar trees, which are actually junipers, not true cedars.
compareHints: Cedar Waxwings are smaller and browner than their rare relative the Bohemian Waxwing, which is grayer overall and has rusty-red under the tail. Bohemian Waxwings also have white and yellow wing markings that Cedars lack, and they're much less common in New England, typically appearing only during irregular winter invasions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bohemian Waxwings are significantly larger than Cedar Waxwings and have much more striking wing patterns with prominent white markings.
